Stalking-by-Notification.short_definition: Using a person's last-seen times, read receipts, story views and online status as evidence in a running case about where they were and why they did not answer.
Stalking-by-Notification.core_meaning: Using a person's last-seen times, read receipts, story views and online status as evidence in a running case about where they were and why they did not answer.
Stalking-by-Notification.expanded_definition: Stalking-by-Notification means turning the small signals apps display, such as a green dot, a 'seen at 2:14' stamp, a story view or a like, into proof of something. The person watching compares those signals with what you said, then brings you the mismatch as a question you have to answer. One hurt remark about being left on read is ordinary. The pattern is the checking repeating, the signals treated like a log, and you starting to time your own replies and posts around the questions. It does not show what anyone meant by looking.
Stalking-by-Notification.plain_language_summary: Someone watches when you are online and then questions you about it. Soon just being seen online feels like something you must explain.
Stalking-by-Notification.why_this_matters: When every green dot can become a question, ordinary use of your own phone turns into something to defend. People start planning when to be online and when to look away, and the hours spent explaining can crowd out the relationship itself.
what_it_is: Reading app signals such as last active, read receipts, typing dots, story views and likes as if they were a record of your day.
Setting those signals beside what you said earlier, then raising any mismatch as a charge: 'You told me you were asleep.'
Asking you to explain rather than telling you how it felt, so the exchange is an inquiry and not a feeling shared.
Coming back in the same week with new dots, so there is always something fresh to bring up.
Sometimes sitting alongside location sharing or checking a shared account, which widens what there is to question.
what_it_sounds_like: I saw you were online at 2am.
You posted a story but couldn't answer me?
It says seen at 11:42. So you read it and just left it.
Why were you active at midnight if you were going to bed?
You liked her photo. Explain that.
Your last seen says 3:10. Who were you talking to?
I'm not checking up on you. It just shows up on my screen.
what_it_is_not: One honest feeling report, such as 'I felt low when I saw you online and hadn't heard back', which asks for comfort and not for an account.
A location-sharing arrangement you both chose, for a long trip or a late commute, that either of you can switch off.
A parent following open household rules about a young child's phone.
Checking when someone does not reply after a flight or a storm, because you are worried they may be hurt.
A passing 'oh, you're up late too' that is left there and not followed by questions.
A work chat status your team agreed means available, used only to see who can pick up a task.
this_may_be_it_when: Questions arrive with exact times attached, which suggests someone has been keeping count.
Your explanation does not close the subject; the next dot becomes the next question.
You are asked to account for likes, follows and story views, not only for unanswered messages.
Saying you would rather not be quizzed about it is answered with something about what you must be hiding.
You switched off read receipts or last-seen, and were then asked why you did.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They say they felt left out and ask for nothing beyond a kind word.
After you explain once, the topic is dropped and not compared with later signals.
They show their own activity as freely and do not mind being asked about it.
The settings were chosen together and either of you can change them.
They apologize for the checking itself when you mention it.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Apps show these signals by default, so everyone sees them whether or not they meant to look.
Someone burned by an earlier relationship may find small signals loud, and be struggling more than charging.
People with different texting rhythms can read the same gap very differently.
In a long-distance relationship, the green dot can be one of the few ways to feel close.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'you're up late!' once, laughing, and moves on.
A parent asking a teenager why there was no reply after a late bus that did not come.
A partner who says 'I saw you online and missed you', which is affection and not an inquiry.
discernment_questions: Is the question 'I felt lonely' or 'explain this timestamp'?
When you explain, does the subject close, or does the explanation become the next thing checked?
Have you changed when you read, like or post because of the questions that follow?
Do they offer the same openness about their own activity?
Is anything beyond the app being watched, such as your location, devices or accounts?
Do the questions get sharper after you spend time with other people?
less_concerning_if: A single hurt remark is followed by 'that wasn't fair of me, I'm just anxious today'.
Both of you can see each other's status and neither of you minds.
They accept your explanation and do not hold it up against later signals.
more_concerning_if: The checking spreads from apps to your location, your devices or your messages.
Questions come with anger, with threats, or with consequences for your money, contact or plans.
You are expected to be reachable at all times and a late reply brings punishment.
pattern_over_time_signs: You answer inside a narrow window and feel a jolt when a notification shows.
You delete likes, hide stories or leave your phone in another room to avoid questions.
Friends notice you reply to them late or in short bursts because you are managing the other conversation.
The list of things that need explaining grows, from replies to likes to who follows you.
Stalking-by-Notification.repair_check: Look at how the dots are treated afterwards. Mending would be them saying the questioning crossed a line, no longer bringing up timestamps, and telling you about worry as worry. A promise to try not to check, while the cross-examinations carry on, has changed nothing.
Stalking-by-Notification.boundary_respect_check: Notice what happens after you decline to explain one timestamp. Does the subject drop, or does the next one arrive within the week? Dropping it is respect. A move from timestamps to your phone, your friends or your accounts points the other way.
Stalking-by-Notification.psychological_mechanism: Silence after a message is an empty space, and a worried mind may fill it with the worst reading. A green dot hands that worry something solid to point at, which can make a stamp on a screen seem like proof. On the other side, each explanation may teach that being visible costs something, so a person starts tidying what shows. The tidying habit may outlast the questions.
Stalking-by-Notification.possible_impact_on_receiver: A flinch when the phone lights up is common, along with composing replies in advance, switching off read receipts and then being asked why, and a sense of being watched from inside your own pocket. Some stop posting, or begin to believe their ordinary habits look suspicious. Others report tiredness from explaining the same hours again.

response_options.soft_clarification: Answer the feeling and leave the timestamp alone: 'It sounds like you felt shut out last night. I was asleep, and I'd like to hear about it when it hurts.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Only if it feels safe to say: 'I'm glad to hear how you feel, but I'm not going to go through who I talked to at what time.' Keep it short and keep your tone level.
response_options.disengagement: Keep replies brief and calm without explaining each time, and do not argue over screenshots. Work out privately, and with an advocate if you can, what you want to do next.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone outside the relationship what gets asked and how often. A domestic abuse advocate or helpline can talk through your options, including how to check your phone and accounts safely.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a manager or colleague quizzes you about your chat status, ask for expectations in writing, such as the hours you are expected to be reachable, and keep dated notes of the questions.

Stalking-by-Notification.boundary_script: "It sounds like it hurt to see me online and not get a reply. That matters to me. I can't go through each time I was on my phone, but I can tell you I'm here and what my evening looks like."
Stalking-by-Notification.safety_note: Watch for the checking moving from apps to your location, your devices or your friends, and for anger or threats when a timestamp does not add up. Sudden privacy changes can be noticed. Before you change any setting, ask a domestic abuse advocate how to check your phone and accounts for tracking in a way that will not alert anyone.
misuse_warning: Calling one sad 'I saw you were online' a form of stalking can turn a vulnerable moment into an accusation. The label fits repeated cross-examination, not a single honest feeling.
The label should not be used to wave away a real worry about trust. It describes how signals are used, not whether any question is allowed.
Stalking-by-Notification.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle also involves watching your online presence, but the person has gone quiet and the watching shows only as a view or a like. Stalking-by-Notification is loud: the signals come back at you as questions. Doxxing publishes private details such as your address to other people, while here the information is whatever the app already displays and the questions stay between the two of you.

Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.short_definition: Going silent in direct messages while still viewing, liking or reacting to someone's posts, so they are neither in contact nor free of it.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.core_meaning: Going silent in direct messages while still viewing, liking or reacting to someone's posts, so they are neither in contact nor free of it.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.expanded_definition: Ghosting is going quiet with no explanation. Orbiting is staying in view afterwards: story views, likes, an occasional emoji reaction. It becomes a cycle when contact fades, the small signals keep arriving, and now and then a warm message returns, often just as you seem to be settling. Someone who simply drifted and never unfollowed can look the same from outside. The shape across weeks matters more than any one view, and none of it shows why anyone does it.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.plain_language_summary: Someone stops answering your messages but keeps watching your stories and liking posts. You can't tell whether the connection is over.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.why_this_matters: You are neither in contact nor free of it. Attention keeps arriving with no reply attached, and each small sign can revive hope at exactly the point it was beginning to fade.
what_it_is: Direct messages that go unanswered or unopened, sometimes for weeks.
Passive signals that continue: story views, likes, a reaction on an old post, a profile visit where the app shows it.
A message that returns after a long gap, warm or casual, and then fades again.
Timing that sometimes lines up with changes in your life, such as a new relationship post or a trip.
A silence that never ends in an ending: no 'I need space', so there is nothing to answer and nothing to accept.
what_it_sounds_like: Three weeks of unanswered messages, yet their name is first in your story viewer list every day.
A heart on a photo from two years ago, the same day you post about a new job.
Hey stranger, I was just thinking about you, arriving after a month of nothing and followed by silence again.
A single emoji reply to your story, with no answer to the question you sent last week.
Messages marked seen within minutes and never answered.
A fresh follow request soon after you muted or unfollowed them.
what_it_is_not: Passive scrolling by someone who simply drifted away and never got round to unfollowing, with no pattern of returns.
A person who said they needed space, even clumsily, and still glances at public posts.
Slow or absent replies from someone who is ill, grieving or overwhelmed and has no energy to write.
An app that puts familiar names at the top of lists, so a view is the algorithm and not a choice.
Two people staying on each other's feeds after an ending both understood, as many do within shared friend groups.
this_may_be_it_when: Silence in messages is complete, but views and likes are regular and prompt.
Reappearances follow signs that you are moving on, such as new photos or a new person.
Each return is friendly but never mentions the silence.
The sequence has gone round at least two or three times.
You catch yourself checking the viewer list for one name.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They told you they needed space, even awkwardly.
Their activity on your accounts fades as the contact fades.
They answer a direct question when you ask one, however late.
The views come through a shared group or event page that many people see.
There is a known reason for absence, such as an illness, a bereavement or a phone ban.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many people scroll through feeds out of habit without choosing whose posts they watch.
Some people find replying hard and still like to see how a friend is; a like is the low-effort contact they can manage.
Shared friend groups mean the same stories reach the same people.
Someone embarrassed about a long silence may find it harder to break each week that passes.
common_false_positives: A friend who is slow to text but likes your posts and then calls you on the weekend.
A cousin who views every story and has never been a texter.
A former partner who liked a birthday photo once.
discernment_questions: Has the silence ever been explained, even once?
Do the contact and the likes return at moments when you are doing better?
If the taps stopped tomorrow, would you feel relief or loss, and what does that tell you about what you need?
Do you find yourself posting with one viewer in mind?
If you asked once, in one line, what they want from contact, would a straight answer come?
less_concerning_if: A direct message eventually brings a plain reply, such as 'I've been avoiding everything lately'.
The passive taps shrink as the silence goes on.
They say plainly that they cannot stay in touch.
more_concerning_if: The taps become more frequent after you mute or limit them, or arrive from other accounts.
They turn up in person or on other platforms after you stop replying.
The silence ends in anger or accusations when you show signs of moving on.
pattern_over_time_signs: You look at who viewed your story before you look at anything else.
You hold off deleting their number, or your own posts, in case they come back.
Months later the same sequence plays: silence, views, a warm message, silence.
Your choices about posting, dating or moving are shaped by whether they might be watching.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.repair_check: Mending would start with a plain account of the silence, in a message that asks nothing of you, and then a clear choice: contact that continues, or a step back that includes not watching. Another warm 'hey' that never mentions the gap is the cycle turning again.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.boundary_respect_check: After you muted, restricted or unfollowed, what became of the views? Signals that stop with no new route opening mean the limit held. A second account, a mutual friend relaying news or a sudden message means it is being tested.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.psychological_mechanism: Intermittent attention can be hard to leave: each small sign arrives unpredictably, and the next one may always be a message. Hope tends to attach to the unanswered part, and the lack of an ending leaves the mind reopening the question. Seeing the name in the viewer list can keep the connection feeling active.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe checking the viewer list, rereading old messages for a clue, and feeling pulled back each time a heart appears. Some describe being unable to grieve a connection that was never formally ended, or hesitating to post, date or move on in case it counts as a reply.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you want a clear answer, ask once in one line: 'Do you want to stay in touch? Either answer is okay.' Treat whatever comes back, or silence, as the answer.
response_options.firm_boundary: Mute or restrict their profile quietly. That stops the viewer list from pulling at your attention, and it needs no announcement.
response_options.disengagement: Stop posting for an audience of one. A close-friends list for stories means you decide who watches, and you can use it without explaining.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend which signs you keep checking for, and ask them to remind you of the facts when you are tempted to read the silence as a message.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague goes silent on direct messages but reacts to everything in the group channel, ask in the channel or by email for what you need to finish the work, so it does not hang on a private thread.

Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.boundary_script: "We haven't talked in a while, and I'm not looking to argue about it. If you want to stay in touch, a direct message to me is the way to do it."
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.safety_note: Silence plus views is usually painful rather than dangerous. It changes if the watching extends to turning up where you are, contacting your family or friends, or messages from new accounts after you block. Anger when you move on is another sign, especially after leaving a controlling relationship. Save dated screenshots somewhere they cannot reach and show them to a stalking or domestic abuse advocate before deciding on a block.
misuse_warning: A like from someone shy or avoidant is not proof of a campaign, and reading every tap as a tactic can keep you watching the list.
Calling someone an 'orbiter' to a shared circle can become a way to shame a person who has simply gone quiet.
Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Stalking-by-Notification turns what it sees into questions and accusations, while orbiting says nothing about what it sees. Doxxing publishes private details to other people, but orbiting stays on your own public posts and reaches only you. The Ghosting-Orbiting Cycle is the one where the contact is gone but the watching, and the occasional warm return, are not.

Brigading.short_definition: A group converging on one person's posts, account or message at once, usually after a shared call to do so, so the volume itself overwhelms them.
Brigading.core_meaning: A group converging on one person's posts, account or message at once, usually after a shared call to do so, so the volume itself overwhelms them.
Brigading.expanded_definition: Brigading is a surge of replies, reports, downvotes, ratings or messages sent to one person or page by people who have been pointed there, often by a post, group chat or forum thread elsewhere. It also happens on review pages, polls and comment sections. What separates it from a pile-on is the shared source and the short window. Each participant may do something small. The weight comes from the sum, which no one can answer one by one.
Brigading.plain_language_summary: Dozens or hundreds of people flood one person with replies or reports within hours. Usually a post somewhere else sent them, and nobody could answer them all.
Brigading.why_this_matters: Volume arriving at once removes any chance of answering the way you could answer a single message, and the platform itself becomes unusable for as long as it lasts. Notifications pile up faster than anyone can read, and a calm reply is buried.
what_it_is: A sudden spike of hostile or mocking replies, ratings or messages in a short window.
A visible source, such as a post, screenshot, group chat or forum thread, that points people toward one person or account.
Mass reports, downvotes or one-star ratings, sometimes on a shop, book or app page.
Participants who may not know the person and have seen only one screenshot.
Sometimes an old post pulled back up and sent round again, so a quiet account is suddenly busy.
what_it_sounds_like: Within minutes of a screenshot being shared in another group, your mentions fill with replies that use the same phrases.
Go and look at what this person said, posted in a group chat, followed by a stream of new commenters.
A run of one-star ratings on your shop page within an hour, none from a buyer.
Replies quoting a screenshot of your post that you cannot find a link to.
Report this account, plus a link, repeated by many users.
Dozens of near-identical replies such as 'Wow. Unbelievable.' from accounts with no history with you.
what_it_is_not: Virality is not coordination: a post that spreads on its own draws unconnected people who arrived by different routes. What marks brigading is convergence traceable to one rallying post or thread, and friends reacting independently to the same post is not that.
Heavy criticism of a public statement from people who each saw it for themselves, in their own words.
An openly announced campaign of letters or calls about a public decision, organized but done in the open under people's own names.
A group of supporters replying warmly to a friend's post, which is coordinated but not an attack.
Real customers leaving many bad reviews after a product actually failed or was recalled.
this_may_be_it_when: You can find the post or thread that points people toward you, or someone sends you the link.
Most replies land within a few hours and then drop off.
Many replies repeat the same wording, screenshot or claim.
The responders have no history with you, and several accounts are new.
Replies are about a clipped or altered version of what you said.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Replies arrive over days, from people with differing views, and some engage with what you actually wrote.
A large account shared your post but asked nobody to respond.
The replies include people you know and the wording varies.
The criticism points at something you did say.
The volume is close to what similar posts from accounts your size get.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Platforms push popular posts to many users at once, which can look like a coordinated wave.
When a news outlet or large account mentions a post, readers arrive together without anyone telling them to.
Strong reactions to a public statement are often shared by people who read the same headline.
Fans of a livestream or show may all react at the same moment.
common_false_positives: A post that went viral on its own merits and drew intense reaction from unconnected people.
A large volume of ordinary criticism after a controversial public statement by a public figure.
Several friends independently reacting to the same public post.
A burst of genuine one-star reviews after a real, widely reported problem.
discernment_questions: Can you find a post, thread or group where people were told to come to you?
Did the replies arrive in a narrow window and fade quickly?
Are people answering what you wrote, or a clipped version you never posted?
Do many share the same phrases or the same screenshot?
Do the responders have any history with you or with one another?
Is the volume unusual for an account your size?
less_concerning_if: The spike fades within a day and the replies are varied.
The source is an open public conversation, not a call to action.
Some people in the thread correct the record on your behalf.
more_concerning_if: Messages reach beyond the post to your email, workplace, family or home.
Threats of violence or your personal details appear in the wave.
The same source sends people to you again and again.
pattern_over_time_signs: A wave returns whenever you post about a particular topic.
Your posts are being screenshotted shortly before each surge.
You mute notifications or close accounts, and the quiet is then cited as proof of something.
People you know start asking about screenshots you have never seen.
Brigading.repair_check: Where the source post's author acknowledges the pile-on, removes the call to converge and asks followers to stop, the volume tends to fall. A quiet deletion while the thread elsewhere keeps running, or an 'I never told anyone to do that' with the link left up, leaves the wave moving.
Brigading.boundary_respect_check: Watch the first day after you limit replies or lock the account. If the wave thins and does not move to your email, workplace or another platform, the limit worked. If new accounts appear or the thread starts discussing how to get round it, the limit is being tested.
Brigading.psychological_mechanism: Seeing many people agree can make a view feel more correct, and each participant can feel their own small reply is harmless because they are one of many. For the person on the receiving end, a flood in a short time can overload the ability to sort real concerns from noise, and the crowd can feel far larger than the number of people actually involved.
Brigading.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dreading to open notifications, losing sleep, deleting posts or accounts, and checking the thread to see what comes next. Some describe shame over things they never said. Friends and employers may see screenshots, so some describe worry about work or reputation, and relief once the wave passes or someone speaks up.

response_options.soft_clarification: If you were misquoted, post one calm correction with the full original attached and answer no individual replies. People who arrive later can then see the record.
response_options.firm_boundary: Use tools that need no announcement: restrict replies, filter keywords, mute the thread and block accounts as they appear.
response_options.disengagement: Step away from notifications for a day. Ask a trusted friend to read them and tell you only about threats or personal details.
response_options.support_seeking: Save dated screenshots of the wave, the rallying post and any threats. Send them to the platform's report tools and, if threats or personal details appear, to the police and an online-harassment support service.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If it may reach your employer, give your manager or HR a short heads-up with screenshots before they find it themselves, and ask who should handle any press or messages.

Brigading.boundary_script: "Here is the original post in full, with what came before it. I'm not answering individual replies."
Brigading.safety_note: Treat threats, a home address, a workplace name or a family member's name appearing in the wave as a different level of problem from rude replies. Save evidence before blocking, report it to the platform and, where threats look credible, to the police. Ask a friend you trust to read the messages for you and flag only threats or personal details.
misuse_warning: Calling any heavy criticism 'brigading' can dismiss people who disagree with you in good faith. The label needs evidence of a shared call to converge.
Accusing a named person of organizing a pile-on without a link or screenshot trail can start a pile-on of its own.
Brigading.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sock Puppets are one person posing as many voices, while a brigade is many real people. Doxxing publishes private details such as an address; a wave can include it, but a brigade needs no private information, only a link to follow. What sets Brigading apart is the shared rallying point: everyone arrives from the same place, at about the same time.

Context Collapse Exploitation.short_definition: Passing on a statement or image without the surrounding material that gave it its meaning, so viewers read something different from what was meant where it began.
Context Collapse Exploitation.core_meaning: Passing on a statement or image without the surrounding material that gave it its meaning, so viewers read something different from what was meant where it began.
Context Collapse Exploitation.expanded_definition: Context Collapse Exploitation is when a screenshot, clip, quote or old post travels without what surrounded it, and the stripped version is used to show something the whole would not show. Examples are a reply without the message it answered, a joke without its setting, or a years-old post shown as a current view. Every excerpt leaves something out, so the question is whether the missing part changes the meaning and whether it was easy to include. It does not show why it was left out.
Context Collapse Exploitation.plain_language_summary: A piece of something you said or posted is cut out of its setting and shared, so people who see only that piece think you meant something you did not.
Context Collapse Exploitation.why_this_matters: The version that circulates is the stripped one, and restoring the context means reaching an audience that has already reacted. By then the first impression has often set, and a correction may not travel as far as the clip did.
what_it_is: A screenshot of one message sent round without the message it replied to.
A quote cut off mid-sentence where the next words change what it says.
A clip trimmed out of a longer talk, joke or sarcastic exchange.
An old post recirculated with its date hidden or ignored, as if it were a current view.
A remark made among friends shown to a public audience that does not share those friends' shorthand.
what_it_sounds_like: A cropped screenshot of one angry-looking reply, captioned: Look how this person talks to people.
A quote that stops at 'I don't think any of us should have to' when the line went on to say 'be afraid to ask for help'.
Here's what they said in 2016. Nothing has changed.
A twelve-second clip of a laugh, captioned as mockery of someone grieving, with the minute before it left out.
A group chat joke posted to a public thread with the line: This is what they really think.
Comments from viewers who saw only the clip: I thought they seemed so nice.
what_it_is_not: People misunderstand context themselves and pass things on innocently, believing the piece they have is complete.
Headlines and short excerpts truncate longer statements as a matter of format, with no attempt to change what was said.
Careless sharing: forwarding something without checking where it came from is a lapse, not a plan.
A fair short quote that does reflect the whole, since all reporting excerpts.
A dated old post pointed out because the person has said the same thing again since.
A screenshot of something that is bad on its own and stays bad when the full thread is read.
this_may_be_it_when: When the full version is added, the meaning flips or shrinks.
The missing part is exactly the part that changes what the excerpt seems to say.
The sharer had the whole thread to hand, because they were in the conversation or the link was public.
Requests for the full original are ignored, removed or answered with 'it doesn't matter'.
The excerpt is posted to an audience likely to react with anger, and not to the person involved.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The sharer posts the full link alongside the excerpt.
The excerpt fairly reflects the longer statement, and the person quoted agrees it does.
The sharer fixes it quickly once shown.
The date and source are shown plainly and the view has not changed.
You have only seen a screenshot of a screenshot and have not yet seen the original.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Platforms show cropped previews, so a shared link may display only a fragment.
People often forward what upset or amused them without checking, believing it was complete.
A screenshot has to fit a screen, so the sender trimmed for size.
Many apps show no date by default, so an old post can look new to the person who shares it.
common_false_positives: A newspaper headline that compresses a long statement into a line.
A friend who forwards half a group chat because it was the funny part.
A single line from a long speech quoted in a caption.
Someone who screenshots your public post to ask what you meant.
discernment_questions: Does the full version change what the piece seems to mean?
Can you find the original, with its link, date and thread, before you react?
Was the missing part easy for the sharer to include?
Does the post ask you to feel something about the person before it shows you the whole?
When the fuller context is shown, does the sharer update or repeat the first version?
less_concerning_if: The sharer corrects the post when shown the fuller version.
The original is linked in the post itself.
The excerpt is clearly labeled as an excerpt.
more_concerning_if: The missing part is the very part that reverses the meaning, and corrections are removed.
The clipped version is used to send people to your employer, school or family.
It travels alongside a pile-on or your personal details.
pattern_over_time_signs: The same account repeatedly posts clipped versions about the same person.
Each correction is met with another clip and never with an update.
You begin to write everything knowing it could be screenshotted, and say less in writing.
People who saw only the clip bring it up with you months later.
Context Collapse Exploitation.repair_check: A proper fix puts the original in full beside the clip, or takes the clip down with a note saying what was left out. A 'for context' reply while the stripped version stays pinned, or a correction placed where far fewer people will see it, leaves the first impression standing.
Context Collapse Exploitation.boundary_respect_check: Ask the sharer to add the full thread or link beside the excerpt, and watch whether it appears and stays. A quick edit is a good sign. Being told the context is irrelevant, or being called defensive for asking, is not.
Context Collapse Exploitation.psychological_mechanism: Viewers judge quickly from whatever is in front of them, and the cut-away part is invisible, so nobody goes looking for it. An excerpt that fits an opinion already held about someone may feel complete, and anger can travel faster than checking. Feeds also put separate audiences in one place, so a joke made for friends reaches strangers with different norms.
Context Collapse Exploitation.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread at learning that a version of them exists that they do not recognize, urgency to explain to people who have already decided, and care about everything they put in writing afterwards. Some withdraw from posting. Some describe messages from acquaintances asking about something they never said.

response_options.soft_clarification: Reply under the post with a link to the full original and one sentence: 'The part before this changes the meaning, so here is the whole thing.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask the poster to add the full thread or take the excerpt down. Keep it short and do not argue the point with commenters.
response_options.disengagement: Do not rewrite the original post or answer every commenter. One pinned correction on your own page is enough.
response_options.support_seeking: Show a friend who has seen neither version the original and the cropped one, and ask what each says to them. Then ask them to share the original when people ask about it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If the excerpt reaches your employer or school, bring the full original with its date and thread to the person who needs it, in writing, before they form a view.

Context Collapse Exploitation.boundary_script: "The screenshot leaves out the message I was replying to. Here is the whole conversation. Please add it next to your post, or take the screenshot down."
Context Collapse Exploitation.safety_note: A clipped quote circulating is a reputation problem, not a physical one. It changes if the clipped version brings threats, your address or workplace being posted, or calls to people who hold power over your income or housing. Save dated copies of both versions and the replies, and take them to the platform's report tool and, if threats appear, the police.
misuse_warning: Saying 'you took it out of context' about every unwelcome quote can protect someone who really did say it. The label needs the missing part to change the meaning.
Accusing a sharer of manipulation when they simply never saw the full conversation turns a mistake into a charge.
Context Collapse Exploitation.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deepfakes fabricate words or images that never existed; here every word is real and the problem is what was left out. Doxxing publishes private facts such as an address, while the material here was often public already. AI Voice Cloning imitates a voice to say new things, but an excerpt keeps the person's real words in a different frame. Context Collapse Exploitation is the one where nothing is invented, only removed.
